questions.prompt: Per Lesson 1, select every statement that is true about what makes a capstone project actually "complete."
options: A working end-to-end pipeline that calls a real LLM API, not a notebook that only runs with hardcoded test inputs on your machine
A measured evaluation with actual numbers, such as retrieval recall or judge scores -- not just "it felt right when I tried it"
A deployed, callable service, containerized and exposed behind a minimal API
A README documenting the architecture, tradeoffs, and what's intentionally out of scope
A fictional company scenario that frames the dataset and users, the same as other capstones in this catalog
questions.explain: Lesson 1 names four concrete bars for "complete": a real end-to-end pipeline hitting a live LLM API, a measured evaluation with real numbers, a deployed/containerized service behind an API, and a README stating architecture, tradeoffs, and scope. The lesson explicitly avoids a fictional company -- the opposite of the last option -- because a capstone is supposed to be genuinely yours, built on documents, data, and tools you chose.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 2's framework, a candidate currently targeting an agentic AI / AI platform engineer role should plan to polish which flagship project deepest, and why?
options: Project 3, because it leans hardest on agent orchestration, security, and operational discipline like approval gates and logging
Project 1, because agentic roles are evaluated mostly on chunking strategy and retrieval metrics
Project 2, because agentic roles are primarily about natural-language-to-SQL generation
None of them -- Lesson 2 says emphasis doesn't matter for this role
questions.explain: Lesson 2 maps each project to a role: Project 3 (a tool-using agent with approval, security, and logging) maps most directly to agentic AI / AI platform engineer roles, since interviewers in that lane probe orchestration, security, and operational discipline specifically -- not retrieval metrics or SQL generation, which belong to Projects 1 and 2.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of chunk overlap in a RAG ingestion pipeline?
options: To keep a passage that straddles a chunk boundary retrievable whole from at least one chunk, at the cost of some duplicated text
To reduce the total number of chunks stored in the vector database
To guarantee every chunk is exactly the same length
To remove the need for an embedding model
To speed up loading chunks into the vector database
To let RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter skip paragraph-boundary splitting entirely
questions.explain: Lesson 4 is explicit: without overlap, a sentence that straddles exactly where one chunk ends and the next begins gets cut in half, and neither chunk alone carries the full idea. A character overlap means the tail of one chunk reappears as the head of the next, so that passage stays retrievable whole from at least one chunk -- at the cost of some duplicated text in the vector database.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B is backwards -- overlap increases the total stored text, since boundary regions are repeated across adjacent chunks, rather than reducing chunk count. Overlap exists to protect meaning at cut points, not to improve storage efficiency.

questions.prompt: A developer calls Qdrant's older `search()` method instead of `query_points` in a new RAG pipeline. What does Lesson 5 say about this choice?
options: `search()` is deprecated and being removed; `query_points` is the current method and should be used instead
`search()` and `query_points` are functionally identical going forward, so either is fine
`search()` is required whenever `with_payload=True` is needed
`query_points` can only be used with embeddings generated by Claude
questions.explain: Lesson 5 states directly that Qdrant's older `search` method is deprecated and being removed, and that the current client uses `query_points` -- so a new pipeline should use `query_points`, not `search()`.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in the system prompt from Lesson 5, instructing the model to say so if the answer isn't in the context gives the model explicit permission to say "I don't know" instead of filling a gap with a plausible-sounding guess -- a risk this path calls ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 5 names this directly: without that instruction, a model may fill a retrieval gap with a plausible-sounding guess instead of admitting it doesn't know -- the hallucination risk this path's RAG & Vector Databases course covered from the start.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about evaluating Project 1's RAG pipeline, per Lesson 6.
options: Recall@k measures whether the chunk actually containing the answer showed up anywhere in the top-k retrieved results
LLM-as-judge scoring is a cheap proxy for human grading, not a full replacement for it -- spot-check some scores by hand
A low recall@5 score means the problem is in generation, so the fix is prompt wording
Re-ranking means retrieving more candidates than needed, then narrowing to the best few with a second pass before generation
"The answers looked fine when I tried a few questions" counts as a real evaluation once you've tried at least ten questions
questions.explain: Recall@k checks whether retrieval surfaced the correct source at all; a low score means the problem is upstream of generation entirely, not something a prompt fix addresses. LLM-as-judge is explicitly called a cheap proxy, not a replacement for human grading. Re-ranking retrieves a larger candidate pool first, then narrows with a second pass. Lesson 6 explicitly rejects "it felt right" as an evaluation at any question count -- only a hand-built eval set with real measured numbers counts.

questions.prompt: Match each Project 1 component to the stack choice that implements it, per Lesson 3.
right: Claude via the Anthropic Messages API
Retrieval recall@k and an LLM-as-judge pass
questions.explain: Lesson 3's stack maps directly: chunking uses RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter, vector storage is Qdrant, generation calls Claude through the Messages API, and evaluation is scored with retrieval recall@k plus an LLM-as-judge pass.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of Project 1's retrieval-and-generation flow, per Lesson 5, in the correct order.
items: Embed the incoming question with the same embedding model used at ingestion time
Query Qdrant's query_points for the top-k closest chunks, with payload included
Assemble a numbered context block that keeps each chunk's source attached
Send the context and question to Claude with a system prompt instructing it to cite sources and say so if the answer isn't in context
Return the generated answer along with its citations
questions.explain: Lesson 5's pipeline runs in exactly this order: embed the question with the ingestion-time embedding model, retrieve the closest chunks from Qdrant via query_points, assemble a numbered and sourced context block, send it to Claude with the grounding system prompt, and return the cited answer.

questions.code:
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
ENV ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=""
CMD ["uvicorn", "api.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]
questions.prompt: Lesson 7's Dockerfile includes the line `ENV ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=""`. What does this line actually do?
options: It documents that the container expects this variable at runtime; it does not bake a real key into the image
It sets the real API key value so the container can call Claude immediately after build
It disables the Anthropic API key requirement entirely
It causes the build to fail unless a real key is supplied at build time
questions.explain: Lesson 7 is explicit that this line exists only to document that the container expects the variable -- it does not set a real value. The actual key is passed at run time (docker run -e ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=...) or through a platform's secret manager; a key baked into a Dockerfile or image layer becomes effectively public the moment the image is pushed anywhere.

questions.prompt: Why does Lesson 9 require connecting the AI data analyst through a dedicated read-only database role, even though queries are already parameterized?
options: Parameterized queries prevent injection through a value, but they don't stop a correctly-parameterized DELETE or UPDATE statement that an LLM might generate -- a read-only role removes write access entirely so there's nothing destructive to run
Parameterization alone is sufficient, and the read-only role is purely a redundant formality with no independent benefit
A read-only role replaces the need for parameterized queries altogether
The read-only role exists only to satisfy a cloud provider's billing requirement, not a security concern
A read-only role is required because SQLite and Postgres cannot run parameterized queries
The read-only role's only purpose is to speed up SELECT queries, not to limit what they can do
questions.explain: Lesson 9 draws this exact distinction: parameterized queries stop SQL injection through a value, but they don't stop a well-formed, correctly-parameterized DELETE or UPDATE that an LLM might still be asked to generate. A role that physically cannot write means even a bad or model-generated query can return wrong results, but it can't destroy anything.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B treats the read-only role as redundant once queries are parameterized, but the lesson explicitly calls these two separate, independent defense layers -- parameterization defends against injected syntax, while the role defends against a syntactically valid but destructive statement. Removing either layer leaves a real gap the other doesn't cover.

questions.prompt: Why does Lesson 10 insist on getting a generated SQL query through a tool_use block instead of asking Claude to "write SQL" and parsing it out of prose?
options: A tool_use block returns the SQL as structured input your code reads directly, rather than something you must reliably regex out of free text, and it keeps your code in control of whether to actually run it
Prose parsing is faster to implement and produces identical reliability
tool_use blocks are required because the Messages API cannot return plain text at all
Parsing prose is actually safer because it avoids JSON Schema validation overhead
questions.explain: Lesson 10 is direct about this: the Messages API's tool-use feature exists for exactly this case -- the SQL comes back as a structured tool_use block, not prose you have to parse, and your own code decides whether to run it. Regexing SQL out of free text is both less reliable and removes that decision point from your code.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Lesson 9's combination of parameterized queries, a least-privilege role, and a statement timeout/row cap means an untrusted or AI-generated query can be wrong, but it can't be ________.
questions.explain: Lesson 9 closes with this exact framing: those three defense-in-depth layers together don't guarantee a generated query is correct -- they guarantee that even a wrong one can't be dangerous.

questions.prompt: A Project 2 SQL result returns 50 rows but only 4 distinct currency codes that need an exchange-rate lookup. Select every statement below that is true per Lesson 11.
options: Calling get_exchange_rate once per row (50 calls) is an N+1 problem -- the same pattern that shows up in database code, moved to the API boundary
Deduplicating to the 4 distinct currency codes before calling the API avoids 46 unnecessary requests
Caching a rate lookup for the duration of the request avoids re-fetching the same code if it's needed again
The correct fix is to let Claude call the API once per row itself, since multi-tool orchestration handles batching automatically
Batching, where the API supports it, could reduce this to a single call for all 4 codes instead of 4 separate ones
questions.explain: Lesson 11 names deduplication, caching, and batching as the three ways to avoid the N+1 trap -- calling an external API once per row instead of once per distinct value actually needed. Multi-tool orchestration, letting Claude decide which tools to call, is a separate concern from N+1 avoidance; it doesn't automatically deduplicate or batch calls on its own, so that option is false.

questions.prompt: Match each Project 2 defense-in-depth layer to what it specifically protects against, per Lesson 9.
left: A hard row limit enforced in code
right: A runaway query (e.g. an unintended cross join) hanging the connection
Untrusted text being interpreted as SQL syntax instead of a data value
A broad query flooding the response with unbounded results
A correctly-parameterized but destructive statement like DELETE or UPDATE
questions.explain: Parameterized queries stop untrusted text from being interpreted as SQL syntax. A read-only role removes the ability to run a correctly-parameterized but destructive statement. A statement timeout turns a runaway query into a fast, visible failure. A hard row limit caps a broad query's result instead of flooding the response.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of Lesson 10's natural-language-to-SQL round trip in the correct order.
items: Send the user's question, the run_sql_query tool definition, and a schema-aware system prompt to Claude
Claude's reply contains a tool_use block with the generated SQL as structured input
Code validates the SQL (SELECT-only, single statement, no banned keywords) before running it
The validated query executes through the read-only, parameterized connection from Lesson 9
The result is sent back as a tool_result block so Claude can generate a natural-language answer
questions.explain: Lesson 10 walks through exactly this five-step round trip: send the schema-aware prompt and tool, receive the generated SQL as a tool_use block, validate it in code before ever running it, execute it through the Lesson 9 safe connection, then send the result back as a tool_result for Claude to turn into a final answer.

questions.prompt: Lesson 12's known-limitations section distinguishes SQL injection (Lesson 9) from a second, separate risk named "prompt injection via the user's question." What is that second risk?
options: A user wording their question in a way that tries to manipulate Claude's reasoning toward an unsafe action, even though the generated SQL itself still passes Lesson 10's validation
A second form of SQL injection that happens only when the API enrichment step is used
An attacker modifying the read-only database role's permissions directly
A vulnerability in the exchange-rate API's own server, unrelated to this project's code
questions.explain: Lesson 12 explicitly separates the two: Lesson 9's validation defends the query text itself, but a determined user could still try to manipulate Claude's reasoning through a cleverly worded question -- a risk the validation layer doesn't catch, since the resulting SQL could still be syntactically valid. Naming that gap honestly is more credible than implying the system is airtight.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 13, which of these best describes why Project 3 carries a different risk profile than Projects 1 and 2?
options: Project 3's agent takes real actions through tools -- sending a message, modifying a record, spending money -- that often can't be undone once executed, unlike Projects 1-2 which only answer questions
Project 3 uses a larger language model than Projects 1 and 2
Project 3 is the only project that uses the Messages API's tool-calling feature
Project 3 has a smaller scope than Projects 1 and 2, so less can go wrong
questions.explain: Lesson 13 draws this distinction directly: Projects 1 and 2 both answer questions, while Project 3 takes actions -- and once a consequential tool call executes, you often can't take it back. That's why it needs a human-approval checkpoint, an audit log, and input validation that Projects 1-2 didn't require in the same way.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 14, the ________ flag that decides whether a tool requires human approval lives in your own application's metadata, not in the tool's Messages API input_schema.
questions.explain: Lesson 14 is explicit that requires_approval is an application-level flag your own code checks, decided at design time per tool -- it is never sent to Claude as part of the tool's input_schema.

questions.prompt: A reviewer rejects a pending issue_refund request. Per Lesson 15, what must happen next for the conversation to continue correctly?
options: A tool_result block must still be sent for that tool_use_id, with is_error: true and an instructive explanation of why it was rejected
No further message is needed -- Claude automatically detects the rejection and moves on
The conversation must restart from scratch with a new system prompt
A plain text message, not a tool_result, should be sent explaining the rejection
questions.explain: Lesson 15 is specific about this: the Messages API expects a tool_result for every tool_use it sent before the conversation can continue -- skipping one produces an error about missing results. A rejection is a valid, real result, sent with is_error: true and an instructive message Claude can act on, not a bare "denied."

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Lesson 16's security and logging layer for Project 3.
options: A tool's input_schema validates shape (e.g., that amount_cents is an integer) but says nothing about whether that value is actually correct
validate_refund_input re-derives the order's authoritative paid total from your own system rather than trusting the model's claim
Validation should run after create_pending_approval, so a reviewer always sees every request regardless of whether the amount is wrong
The audit log should record rejected and failed-validation cases, not just successful executions
Logging every tool call replaces the need for the approval workflow from Lesson 15
questions.explain: Schema validation only checks type and shape, not truth -- a type-valid amount_cents can still be wrong. validate_refund_input re-fetches the real paid total and checks the model's claim against it, and this check runs before create_pending_approval, so a reviewer should never even see a request with a bad number. The audit log should capture rejected and failed-validation cases, not just successes. Logging doesn't replace approval -- Lesson 16 explicitly says both layers are needed together.

questions.prompt: Match each piece of Project 3's agent state to where Lesson 17 says it must live once the agent is deployed.
right: Passed as environment variables at runtime, never baked into the image
requirements.txt, installed during the image build
A real database table, not an in-memory dict
Durable storage such as a database table or shipped log pipeline, not just stdout
questions.explain: Lesson 17 is explicit that pending approvals belong in a real database table (an in-memory dict loses them on restart), audit log entries belong in durable storage rather than stdout (container logs get rotated or lost), secrets like ANTHROPIC_API_KEY are passed as environment variables at runtime, and the Dockerfile installs dependencies from requirements.txt during the build.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of Project 3's approval workflow, per Lesson 15, in the correct order.
items: Claude's response contains a tool_use block for issue_refund
The dispatcher checks the requires_approval flag and creates a pending approval record instead of executing anything
A reviewer sees the pending request's input and reason, and approves or rejects it
On approval, the real tool executes and its result is sent back as a tool_result; on rejection, an is_error: true result explaining why is sent instead
Claude's next response reflects whichever outcome actually happened
questions.explain: Lesson 15's flow runs in exactly this order: Claude proposes the sensitive tool call, the dispatcher pauses execution and records a pending approval rather than running anything, a human reviewer decides, and only then does either the real tool run (approved) or an informative is_error result get sent (rejected) -- with Claude's final response reflecting whichever actually happened.

questions.prompt: In Lesson 14's worked example, why must look_up_order run before issue_refund is ever called?
options: issue_refund's own tool description says it should only be used after look_up_order confirms the order and amount, and it must never refund more than the original paid total
The Messages API enforces tool call ordering automatically based on each tool's name
look_up_order is required because issue_refund has no input_schema of its own
Without look_up_order, Claude cannot generate a tool_use block of any kind
questions.explain: issue_refund's description states this explicitly: "Only use after look_up_order confirms the order and amount. Never use to refund more than the original paid total." This is a convention written into the tool's own description, not something the Messages API enforces mechanically -- Claude follows it because the description tells it to.

questions.prompt: Why does Lesson 18 insist the Project 3 demo show a rejected tool call, not only an approved one?
options: An agent that only ever gets approved doesn't prove the checkpoint actually works -- it proves the rejection path was never tested
Approved calls cannot be demonstrated live, so the rejected path is the only one available to show
Showing a rejection is required by the Messages API's terms of use
A rejected call produces a different, more impressive-looking tool_use block
questions.explain: Lesson 18 makes this point directly: demonstrating only the approved path doesn't actually prove the approval checkpoint works, since that's the easy case. Showing a question trigger the sensitive tool, walking through the pending approval, rejecting it live, and showing Claude's response to the is_error result is what proves the safety mechanism actually blocks something.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 19, what are the three proof points an AI engineering resume needs to carry, given that there's no universal certification to lean on?
options: Something deployed, something evaluated with a real number, and something documented in a README a stranger could follow
A list of every model provider's API the candidate has called
A certification from each AI framework used
A single flagship project with no evaluation numbers, since deployment alone is sufficient
questions.explain: Lesson 19 names exactly three proof points: something you deployed (not just ran in a notebook), something you evaluated (a real number, not a claim), and something you documented (a README a stranger could read and understand your decisions from).

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Lesson 19's resume-bullet pattern names what you did, what you actually produced, and what technique or tool you used -- the ________ + artifact + framework pattern.
questions.explain: Lesson 19 calls this the action + artifact + framework pattern: a strong bullet states the action taken, a concrete artifact a reviewer could ask to see, and the specific technique or framework used -- vague verbs like "worked on" give a reviewer nothing to follow up on.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about presenting a capstone project in a portfolio, per Lesson 20.
options: A strong README front-loads a one-sentence description, an architecture diagram or bullet list, a demo link, eval results, and key design decisions, in that order
A demo video should be linked near the top of the README, not buried at the bottom
Pinning a clear, unmodified tutorial clone with no original README is a strong way to fill GitHub's pinned-repo slots
A reviewer has no way to judge "it works" without a measured result to look at
GitHub allows up to six pinned repositories, so the goal is three complete projects, not thirty shallow ones
questions.explain: Lesson 20 lists the five-part README order (description, architecture, demo link, eval results, design decisions), says a demo link belongs near the top, and states plainly that a reviewer has no way to judge quality without a real measured number. It also explicitly warns that pinning a tutorial clone with no original README "signals the opposite of what you want," and says to pin three deep projects into GitHub's six pinned-repo slots, not thirty shallow ones.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 21, what is the reliable method for answering an AI engineering interview question, rather than reciting a memorized script?
options: Name the real tradeoff, state your default, then name the condition that would change your answer
Give the single most technically impressive-sounding answer available, regardless of tradeoffs
Describe a fabricated incident that makes the tradeoff concrete, even if it didn't actually happen
Always defer to whatever framework the interviewer mentions first
questions.explain: Lesson 21 states this method directly, and explicitly warns against inventing a "war story" to recite, since a made-up incident falls apart under one follow-up question. Naming the real tradeoff and the condition that would change the answer signals stronger reasoning than either a confident one-liner or an unfocused list of options.

questions.prompt: Put these four parts of Lesson 22's AI system design framework in the order they should be addressed.
items: Requirements -- scale, latency tolerance, data freshness, and the cost of being wrong
Architecture -- the real components and how data flows between them
Tradeoffs -- the two or three decisions that actually matter, each defended with a default
Failure modes -- what goes wrong at each step, paired with the safeguard that catches it
questions.explain: Lesson 22's framework runs requirements first (what you're actually building for), then architecture (the real components and data flow), then tradeoffs (the decisions that matter, each with a defended default), and finally failure modes -- the step the lesson says most candidates skip, even though it's the one that signals real production experience.

questions.prompt: Why does Lesson 23 deliberately avoid quoting a specific AI engineering salary figure?
options: Salary figures go stale quickly and vary enormously by market, company stage, and even which part of the AI stack a role focuses on, so the lesson teaches the research process instead of a number that might already be wrong
AI engineering salaries are the same everywhere, so a single number would already cover every case
Salary negotiation isn't relevant to AI engineering roles
The lesson assumes every reader already knows their market rate from a previous course
questions.explain: Lesson 23 explains this directly: salary figures go stale fast and vary by country, metro area, company stage, and even which part of the AI stack a role focuses on, and the catalog has no reliable way to verify a precise number as current. Instead it teaches building your own range from live sources -- aggregated salary sites, government labor data, and real job postings under multiple title variants.
